short: Hernán Cortés, named in Keats’s sonnet about Homer.
note: Hernán Cortés, the Spanish conqueror of Mexico, appears as “stout Cortez” in John Keats’s On First Looking into Chapman’s Homer (1816), a sonnet comparing the discovery of poetry to geographical exploration.

sources.label: John Keats · On First Looking into Chapman’s Homer

term: Miss Minerva and William Green Hill
short: Frances Boyd Calhoun’s novel about an aunt and nephew.
note: A novel by Frances Boyd Calhoun about the strict Miss Minerva and her mischievous young nephew, William Green Hill.

short: The sea nymphs of Greek mythology.
note: Sea nymphs, traditionally fifty daughters of Nereus and Doris, associated with the Mediterranean Sea and the company of Poseidon.
Nymphs of mountains and mountain woods; Greek oreias means a mountain-dwelling nymph.

sources.label: Theoi · Dryads and Oreads, classical source passages

note: Nymphs associated with trees and woods. The name comes from Greek drys, oak or tree.
Ash-tree nymphs. Hesiod’s Theogony describes their birth from Earth after the blood of the wounded Uranus fell upon her.
Naiads: nymphs of springs, streams, rivers, lakes, and other fresh waters in Greek mythology.

short: Possibly Thoë, one of the Nereids in Homer.
note: Possibly Thoë, a sea nymph named among the daughters of Nereus in Book 18 of Homer’s Iliad.

short: Heinrich Schliemann, excavator of Troy and Mycenae.
note: Heinrich Schliemann (1822–1890), the archaeologist associated with major nineteenth-century excavations at Troy, Mycenae, and other prehistoric sites.

sources.label: American School of Classical Studies at Athens · Heinrich Schliemann

note: A Greek designation for the nymphs of rivers, alongside the related term potameides.

sources.label: Jennifer Larson · Greek Nymphs: Myth, Cult, Lore, p. 8

short: Rudolph Dirks’s comic strip about mischievous children.
note: An American newspaper comic created by Rudolph Dirks, inspired by Wilhelm Busch’s Max and Moritz, the German picture-book account of two mischievous boys.

sources.label: Library of Congress · Max and Moritz and The Katzenjammer Kids
